title: Text Structure and Purpose
lead: These questions give you a short text and ask about the text itself, not the facts in it. There are three versions: “Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?”, “Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?”, and “Which choice best states the function of the underlined sentence?” All three ask you to look past what the text says and see why and how it says it.

parts.title: Part 1 · Purpose and structure
parts.html:
Purpose is the why. It is the reason the author wrote the text and what the reader is meant to come away with. A purpose is easiest to state as a verb plus a topic:

  • to explain how something works
  • to illustrate a claim with a case
  • to criticize an idea
  • to argue for a position
  • to introduce a person, a work or a finding

After reading, ask yourself what you now understand or believe that you did not before. That takeaway is usually the purpose.

Structure is the how. It is the route the text takes to reach its purpose: where it starts, where the focus moves, and what gets the emphasis. Structure is easier to see when you look at how the ideas relate. Does the second idea disagree with the first? Does one cause the other, or build on it? Those relationships give the text its shape.

parts.title: Part 2 · The method for whole-text questions
parts.html:
1. Check the task. Glance at the question first. “Main purpose” and “overall structure” are close relatives, but it helps to read with the right one in mind.
  2. Summarize the text. Read closely and reduce the whole text to one or two plain points in your own words. This is the step that does the work.
  3. Test the choices against your summary. A summary is not the same thing as a purpose or a structure, but the right choice will look a lot like it. A correct purpose names the main ideas of the text. A correct structure usually reads like your summary with the details taken out.

parts.title: Part 3 · Worked example: overall structure
parts.html:
The following text is from Charlotte Perkins Gilman’s 1910 poem “The Earth’s Entail”.

No matter how we cultivate the land,
Taming the forest and the prairie free;
No matter how we irrigate the sand,
Making the desert blossom at command,
We must always leave the borders of the sea;
The immeasureable reaches
Of the windy wave-wet beaches,
The million-mile-long margin of the sea. Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
A) The speaker provides examples of an admirable way of approaching nature and then challenges that approach.
B) The speaker describes attempts to control nature and then offers a reminder that not all nature is controllable.
C) The speaker argues against interfering with nature and then gives evidence supporting this interference.
D) The speaker presents an account of efforts to dominate nature and then cautions that such efforts are only temporary.

Summarize. Lines 1–4 share one pattern and are not a complete thought. “No matter how” sets up a contrast: however much we shape the land… Lines 5–8 finish the thought by stressing how vast the sea is: …we cannot shape the sea.

Put together: we can control and reshape the land, but we cannot control the sea. That sentence is the structure, once the poetic language is removed.

Test the choices.

  • A calls the approach “admirable”. The poem is not about good or bad; it is about possible or impossible.
  • C says the speaker argues against interfering with nature. The poem never says interfering is wrong, and the second half gives no evidence supporting interference.
  • D gets the first half right, which makes it tempting. But the second half does not say the efforts are “temporary”. It says that with the sea they cannot succeed at all.
  • B matches both halves: some of nature can be controlled, some cannot. It is the summary in other words, and it is the answer.

parts.title: Part 4 · Underlined-sentence questions
parts.html:
Here one sentence or phrase is underlined and the question asks for its function in the text as a whole. It is the same skill, aimed at one part. Two questions settle it:

  • What information is in the underlined part?
  • What does that information do for the rest of the text?
  1. Summarize the text in one or two points, paying extra attention to the underlined part. Once you understand the whole, the job of the part is much easier to see.
  2. Predict the function in your own words. Compare the underlined part with what comes just before and just after. Does it introduce what follows? Does it contradict what came before? Does it give an example or a reason?
  3. Test the choices against your prediction and take the closest match.

Tip. Stay inside the underline. A wrong choice often describes correctly what a different sentence in the text does. Make sure the choice is about the underlined words and nothing else.

parts.title: Part 5 · Worked example: function of a sentence
parts.html:
The following text is from Herman Melville’s 1854 novel The Lightning-rod Man.

The stranger still stood in the exact middle of the cottage, where he had first planted himself. His singularity impelled a closer scrutiny. A lean, gloomy figure. Hair dark and lank, mattedly streaked over his brow. His sunken pitfalls of eyes were ringed by indigo halos, and played with an innocuous sort of lightning: the gleam without the bolt. The whole man was dripping. He stood in a puddle on the bare oak floor: his strange walking-stick vertically resting at his side. Which choice best states the function of the underlined sentence in the overall structure of the text?
A) It sets up the character description presented in the sentences that follow.
B) It establishes a contrast with the description in the previous sentence.
C) It elaborates on the previous sentence’s description of the character.
D) It introduces the setting that is described in the sentences that follow.

Summarize. A stranger is standing in a cottage. Then comes the underlined sentence. Everything after it describes how he looks: thin, gloomy, tired eyes, soaking wet. The text as a whole is a description of an unknown man.

Decode the underlined sentence. The words are old-fashioned, but each can be worked out: “singularity” means he is unusual, “impelled” means pushed someone to act, “scrutiny” means careful looking. In plain words: he was so strange that you had to look at him more closely.

Predict. The sentence turns the reader’s attention to the stranger’s appearance, which the following sentences then describe.

Test the choices.

  • B claims a contrast. The sentence before only says where he is standing, and nothing contradicts that.
  • C says the sentence elaborates on a description. The underlined sentence contains no description itself; the description comes after it.
  • D is about the setting. Apart from the word “cottage”, the text does not describe the setting at all.
  • A matches the prediction: the sentence sets up the description that follows. It is the answer.

parts.title: Part 6 · Tips that save points
parts.html:
TipHow to use it
Stay specificReject a choice that brings in something the text never discusses, and a choice that makes a side detail sound like the main point.
Be strict with two-part choicesStructure choices usually split the text in two (“does X, and then does Y”). Both halves must be accurate. If the first half fits and the second is slightly off, the choice is wrong.
Be strict with function choicesA choice can describe the underlined part correctly and still get its role in the whole text wrong. One detail that does not match is enough to eliminate it.
Follow the transitionsWords like however, therefore and no matter show how one idea leads to the next. Note them as you read; they are the joints of the structure. Class 23 covers transitions in full.

The reading habits from Class 1 apply here too: strip the details, do not stall on a hard word, shorten the jargon, and eliminate before you guess.

parts.title: Part 7 · Worked example: main purpose
parts.html:
The following text is from Maggie Pogue Johnson’s 1910 poem “Poet of Our Race.” In this poem, the speaker is addressing Paul Laurence Dunbar, a Black author.

Thou, with stroke of mighty pen,
Hast told of joy and mirth,
And read the hearts and souls of men
As cradled from their birth.
The language of the flowers,
Thou hast read them all,
And e’en the little brook
Responded to thy call. Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
A) To praise a certain writer for being especially perceptive regarding people and nature
B) To establish that a certain writer has read extensively about a variety of topics
C) To call attention to a certain writer’s careful and elaborately detailed writing process
D) To recount fond memories of an afternoon spent in nature with a certain writer

Stay specific. Three choices bring in things the poem does not say:

  • B takes “read” literally. In the poem Dunbar “reads” hearts, souls and flowers, which is a figure of speech for understanding them, not for reading books.
  • D turns the nature images into a real afternoon outdoors. No such event is described.
  • C is positive, like the poem, but it is about his writing process. The poem admires his ability and never mentions how he works.

That leaves A: the poem praises a writer for how well he understands people and nature.

Do not stall on a hard word. You may not know “mirth”, but it is paired with “joy” in a poem of praise, so it must mean something similar. Even without that guess, eliminating the three choices that do not match the text gets you to the answer.

parts.title: Part 8 · What it says and why it is there
parts.html:
The usual way to miss a function question is to reread the underlined sentence, understand it perfectly, and then find that no choice seems to match. The choices do not describe what the sentence says. They describe why it is there.

Turn the question into a plainer one: “What point is this sentence there to support?”

  • Where to look. The point a sentence serves is usually stated before it, and sometimes just after. Read one sentence on each side. If the underlined part is near the start of the text, begin from the first sentence, which usually holds the main point.
  • Expect general wording. The text says “the bridge” and the choice says “a structure”; the text names a scientist and the choice says “a researcher”. Keep the topic in mind so that you recognise it in this more abstract form.

Main point and main purpose are different things.

Main pointMain purpose
What it isWhat the text claimsWhat the text does
How it is wordedA statementA verb and its object: “to explain…”, “to describe…”, “to challenge…”
ExampleStreet trees lower summer temperatures in cities.To present a benefit of a feature of cities

If you know the main point, the purpose is usually one short step away. Do not be thrown when the correct choice does not repeat the point and instead names the kind of thing the text is doing.

Use the first sentence. In a text this short, the first sentence very often shows the purpose by itself. Read all of it carefully, form a guess, then skim the rest to confirm.

For structure questions, check one part at a time. The choices look long, but each has two halves (“it presents X, then explains Y”). Decide what the text does at the end, and cross out every choice whose second half says something else.

parts.title: Part 9 · Signal words and answer verbs
parts.html:
Function questions are built at the places where ideas meet: where something new is introduced or the direction changes. Particular words and punctuation marks announce what a sentence is doing.

You seeThe sentence is probably there to
for example, for instanceillustrate the point just made
because, the reason is, a colon, a dashexplain
however, but, yet, in contrastcontrast, or introduce the idea the text prefers
indeed, in fact, italics, a repeated wordemphasize
may, might, could, perhapsspeculate or suggest a possibility
a term in quotation marks; “but is this really so?”express doubt
therefore, thus, as a resultdraw a conclusion
parentheses, a pair of dashesadd a side detail or a limit

The verbs in the choices have a charge. A text that approves of its subject will not have a function such as “to criticize”, and a text that raises a doubt will not have “to celebrate”. Checking the charge often removes two choices at once.

PositiveNegativeNeutral
support, illustrate, emphasize, explain, defendchallenge, question, criticize, dispute, cast doubt ondescribe, present, introduce, summarize, note

Extreme verbs are rarely right. Prove, disprove, attack, condemn, mock: science and social science texts discuss ideas that are taken seriously and not yet settled, so a choice claiming that something is proved or attacked usually goes too far.

Example. Beavers are often treated as pests because their dams flood farmland. In dry regions, however, the ponds behind those dams keep streams flowing through the summer. Ecologists in Nevada found that valleys with beaver dams stayed green during a drought that browned the land around them.

Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole? A) It describes the damage that beaver dams cause to farmland.
B) It presents a benefit of beaver dams that contrasts with a common view of the animals.
C) It proves that beavers should be protected in every region.
D) It questions the methods used in a study of beaver dams. Signal: “however” turns away from the first sentence, which gave the common, negative view.
Charge: the underlined sentence is positive about the dams, so A and D are out.
Extreme: C says “proves” and “every region”; the sentence speaks only of dry regions.
B names both the benefit and the contrast.
